measures.methodNote: Headline = count of counties with RUCC 4-9 (nonmetro). Row value = RUCC code 1-9 (1-3 metro by size of metro area; 4-9 nonmetro by urban population and adjacency to a metro area).
measures.methodology: USDA's Rural-Urban Continuum Codes sort every county into nine groups: three metro groups by the size of the metro area and six nonmetro groups by the size of the county's urban population and whether it borders a metro area. The 2023 codes use 2020 Census population and the 2023 OMB metro definitions. A county is classified as a whole, so a metro county can contain rural places and a nonmetro county can contain a small city.

measures.label: Kentuckians living in rural areas (Census definition)
measures.methodNote: Statewide = sum of POP_RUR (1,860,980) / sum of POP_COU (4,505,836) over KY counties. Row value = POPPCT_RUR x 100. 1,220,368 of the rural residents live in nonmetro counties and 640,612 in metro counties. The state's RHTP abstract gives 41.6% (1.87 million).
measures.methodology: The Census Bureau classifies each census block as urban or rural; everyone outside a 2020 urban area (generally 5,000+ people or 2,000+ housing units) counts as rural. This is the kind of definition behind the senator's 42%. It is a place-based count, so it includes rural residents of metro counties.

measures.label: Counties with ambulance deserts (as reported by EMS advocates)
measures.methodNote: Reported as 'nearly 92%' of Kentucky counties (about 110 of 120); the county list and method were not published with the figure.
measures.proxyFor: Share of each county's population living more than 25 minutes from an ambulance station
measures.methodology: The figure comes from the Kentucky Emergency Response Alliance, an EMS advocacy coalition, as reported by the Kentucky Lantern, and uses the Maine Rural Health Research Center definition: people living more than 25 minutes from the nearest ambulance station. A county counts if any part of it is a desert, so the figure does not say how many residents are affected. The underlying national study (Jonk et al., 2023) used 2021-2022 station locations for 41 states, and its authors say missing station data make it an undercount.
measures.comparability: Secondary figure from an advocacy source, not a published county table. It counts counties with any desert area, not the share of residents, and should not be read as 90% of Kentuckians lacking ambulance access.

measures.label: Primary care doctors per 100,000 people
measures.methodNote: Rate = v004_numerator / v004_denominator x 100,000. Rows: 2022 rate (value), 2012 rate from the CHR trend file (per100k2012) and the change; 68 of 120 counties had a lower rate in 2022 than in 2012. Series = statewide rate by data year (2010-2021 trend file; 2022 supplement). Rows carry physician counts so the UI can re-aggregate.
measures.methodology: Counts active, non-federal MDs and DOs under 75 whose primary specialty is family medicine, general practice, general internal medicine or general pediatrics, placed by practice address (AMA Physician Masterfile via HRSA's Area Health Resources File). It covers all payers, not only doctors who see Medicaid patients, and excludes nurse practitioners and physician assistants. Small counties swing with one doctor arriving or leaving. Each year uses its own population estimate.

measures.methodNote: Headline = PCPs in RUCC 4-9 counties (773) / all KY PCPs (2845). Row value = PCPs per 100,000 residents in the county group. Series = the same share for 2012 (trend file) and 2022.
measures.proxyFor: Share of primary care physicians practicing in Census-rural areas (the definition behind '42% rural')
measures.methodology: Same physician count as the county PCP measure (AMA Masterfile via HRSA AHRF, all payers), summed over USDA nonmetro counties. The senator's '17% of PCPs' could not be reproduced: by county, about 27% of primary care doctors practice in nonmetro counties, which hold about 38% of residents. A lower share is possible under a block-level (Census) rural definition, because doctors in nonmetro counties cluster in the county seat, but no public file places physicians at that level.
measures.comparability: County-based rural definition (USDA nonmetro). The senator's 42% rural figure uses the Census block-level definition, so the two halves of his comparison may rest on different definitions.

measures.label: Counties short of primary care, by type of shortage designation

rows.label: Whole county, geographic or high-needs geographic HPSA
Whole county, population-group HPSA only (low-income or similar)

measures.methodNote: Each county is placed in the first category it meets, in row order. Whole county = an active Single County component of a geographic, high-needs geographic or population HPSA; part of county = census-tract components only; facility only = only FQHC, look-alike, RHC or correctional designations. Whole-county total = 108; any area designation (whole + part) = 112; counties with any geographic designation (whole or tract) = 38.
measures.methodology: HRSA designates a Health Professional Shortage Area when the ratio of residents to primary care physicians passes a threshold (generally 3,500:1 for a geographic area, 3,000:1 for a population group such as low-income residents). A geographic HPSA means everyone in the area counts as underserved; a population HPSA means only a group (usually low-income or Medicaid-eligible residents) does; tract-level designations cover only part of a county. Facility designations (most health centers and rural health clinics) are automatic and say nothing about the county.

measures.methodNote: For each June 30, counts KY counties with an area HPSA (geographic, high-needs geographic, population) Single County component whose HPSA Designation Date is on or before that date and whose Withdrawn Date is blank or later. anyArea adds census-tract components. measures.proxyFor: HRSA point-in-time designation counts as published on each date
measures.methodology: HRSA does not publish a county count over time, so this is rebuilt from the dates in today's designation file. It can miss designations withdrawn long ago if HRSA has purged them, and a re-designation carrying a new ID shows only its newest date, so early years may be understated. The whole-county count was 107 in the 2023 and 2024 snapshots and 108 in 2026.

measures.label: What Medicaid paid per office visit, by how deprived the county is

comparison.label: Kentucky, all office visits (paid per line)

measures.methodNote: Headline = most deprived quarter minus least deprived quarter, dollars per visit (-3.40, -8.8%). The 120 KY counties are ordered by 2022 SDI score (ties broken by the unrounded SDI value, then FIPS) and split into four groups of 30. Row value = line-weighted mean of county mix-adjusted paid per visit (see office-visit-paid-per-visit-by-county) over counties not suppressed; paidPerLineRaw is the unadjusted group paid / lines; countyMedian is the unweighted median county value. Correlations use one point per non-suppressed county, unweighted; p-values are approximate (t distribution). Sensitivity: Spearman rho vs SDI for counties with 1,000+ lines = -0.059 (n=116); line-weighted Pearson r vs SDI = -0.424.
measures.averaging: line-weighted mean of county mix-adjusted paid per line (all lines, including zero-paid)
measures.finding: Across Kentucky counties there is no meaningful relationship between deprivation and what Medicaid paid per office visit after adjusting for visit mix (Spearman rho -0.06 against the SDI, -0.07 against the CDC SVI); practices in the most deprived quarter of counties were paid $35.08 per visit against $38.48 in the least deprived quarter (-8.8%), a gap that comes from how the highest-volume counties are paid (line-weighted r -0.42) rather than a county-by-county pattern (the median county in the most deprived quarter was paid $35.78, against $36.19 in the least deprived).
measures.proxyFor: Medicaid allowed amount per office visit by member deprivation (member ZCTA or block group ADI)
measures.methodology: Groups Kentucky counties into four equal groups by the Social Deprivation Index (a national ranking of counties built from seven census measures) and shows the average Medicaid paid per office-visit line for practices located in each group, adjusted for the mix of visit levels. Kentucky Medicaid pays one statewide fee per code, so differences here come from which practices bill (clinic type, payer mix among the managed care plans, zero-paid lines) rather than from the fee schedule. Practice location is not patient residence, and rural health clinics and health centers paid per encounter can understate what is paid. The correlation figures show how closely county payment tracks deprivation; a value near 0 means no consistent relationship.
measures.comparability: The SDI ranks counties nationally; the CDC SVI used for the second correlation ranks counties only within Kentucky. Both describe all residents, not Medicaid members.

notes: Senator's figures vs. data (Sen. Meredith, 0:12:18-0:12:36 and 0:24:11). (1) '42% rural': supported. The 2020 Census counts 41.3% of Kentuckians as rural (block-level definition); the state's RHTP abstract says 41.6% (1.87 million). By county (USDA nonmetro), 38.2% live in the 81 rural counties. (2) '17% of PCPs': not reproduced. By county, 27.2% of primary care physicians practice in nonmetro counties (2022, AMA/AHRF), down from 31.6% in 2012, against 38.1% of residents; nonmetro counties have 45.0 PCPs per 100,000 vs. 74.2 in metro counties. (3) '107 of 120 HPSA counties' vs. DecisionPro's '112 of 120' (hpsa-primary-care-counties in access.json): both are cuts of the same HRSA file. 112 = counties with any active primary care area designation, whole county or census-tract part. Today 108 are whole-county designations and 4 are part-county only, so 112 = 108 + 4. The senator's 107 matches the whole-county count in the 2023 and 2024 snapshots reconstructed from HRSA designation dates (hpsa-primary-care-whole-county-trend); one more county was added by mid-2025. Only 36 counties are whole-county geographic or high-needs geographic HPSAs (everyone counts as underserved); the other 72 whole-county designations cover a population group (low-income residents). 3 counties have only facility designations and 5 have none. Suggested tile wording: '112 counties have a primary care shortage designation (108 countywide, 4 in part); 36 are short for all residents.' (4) '90% ambulance deserts': consistent with the advocacy figure (nearly 92% of counties, about 110), which counts counties with any area beyond 25 minutes of a station, not the share of residents. The resident share by county is unresolved. Scenario inputs for plan #12/#6 (no scenario computed here): pool = physician-professional-paid-tmsis (CY 2023 CPT professional payments, $2.06B; office visits alone $314M with county rows in office-visit-paid-by-county); weights = social-deprivation-index-county (ADI unresolved); fee level = medicaid-to-medicare-fee-index (primary care 0.54 of Medicare, 2024); current gap = rural-urban-office-visit-payment-gap. The CMS-64 FFS physician line ($40M) is not the pool, because most Kentucky physician payments flow through MCO capitation. T-MSIS figures use billing-practice location, not member residence. PCP county rows carry physician counts so the UI can re-aggregate for any grouping. Census figures come from the 2020_UA_COUNTY file because the Census API now requires a key.
